default.$description:
The hairline — every panel edge, table rule, input border, card border, divider. A themeable ROLE rather than one component's internal geometry: re-point it to --border-width-200 and the whole kit gets heavier chrome in one move.

This token spent its life carrying the argument for why it had no siblings, and lost that argument twice. It read: 'An `emphasis` sibling is deliberately absent — the remaining 2px borders in the kit are all micro-geometry (spinner rings, the kbd keycap lip, a chevron built from two borders).' That enumeration was the whole case, and it was incomplete both times it was tested. `focus` broke it first (see that token). `emphasis` broke it on 2026-08-16: esa-file-upload's dropzone edge is 2px dashed, which is not micro-geometry but a deliberate invitation — the one border in the kit whose job is to say 'drop here', and the only one that reads as a target rather than a division.

The lesson is about the SHAPE of the argument, not the count. 'No component needs this' is a claim about a survey, and a survey is a snapshot; it ages every time a component is added, and it fails silently because nothing re-runs it. SPEC.md's rule that a role must have a reader is still right — what was wrong was treating an enumeration written once as if it stayed true.

emphasis.$description:
A border heavy enough to read as a TARGET rather than a division. The hairline divides; this one asks for something. Currently one reader — esa-file-upload's dropzone, `2px dashed` — and one reader is the bar SPEC.md sets, not a shortfall: the role exists because a real border needed it, which is exactly the test that kept it out of the system until now.

Why this is a role and not a component hook: a spoke re-skinning its chrome weight wants its drop targets to move WITH the rest of its borders, one step heavier. A --file-upload-border-width would move alone and drift out of relation to --border-width-default every time a theme touched one and not the other. The pair is the point — emphasis is 'default, but louder', and a theme that doubles its chrome should double both.

Distinct from `focus` despite sharing 2px today. Focus is an accessibility affordance on the element the user is ON; emphasis is a resting state of the element itself, present before any interaction. A spoke thickening its focus ring for contrast has said nothing about its dropzones, and collapsing them would make that one decision silently two.

What does NOT belong here: the 2px in spinner rings, the collapsible chevron, the slider thumb, and the color-picker's `2px solid transparent` forced-colors affordance. Those are micro-geometry — the number is load-bearing for a specific shape, and re-pointing them at a role would deform the shape rather than re-theme it.

Value-neutral: 2px before and after, so no component changes appearance.

focus.$description:
The focus ring's thickness. Pairs with --color-border-default-focus exactly as --border-width-default pairs with --color-border-default: one role per property, so a theme can move the ring's weight and its colour independently. Tier 3's --focus-ring-width now reads this instead of holding a bare 2px, which is the same shape --focus-ring-color has always had (a thin tier-3 alias over a tier-2 role) — width was simply never given the tier-2 half.

This role was rejected once, and the rejection is worth recording because its PREMISE was wrong rather than its reasoning. The argument against an `emphasis` width was that every 2px border in the kit is micro-geometry — spinner rings, the kbd keycap lip, a chevron. The focus ring was not in that enumeration and does not fit it: 33 components render it, more than read any other tier-3 token, and it is not micro-geometry but an accessibility affordance whose weight is a legitimate brand axis (a spoke that needs a heavier ring for contrast has to be able to reach it). It is also not a `border` in any component — every consumer paints it with `outline` or `box-shadow` — which is precisely why a survey of BORDERS missed it. The name still says `border` because tier 2 already calls the ring's colour --color-border-default-focus; the two should agree, and renaming that is a separate argument.

Value-neutral: 2px before and after, so no component changes appearance.
